sections.title: Floorsight
sections.note: Existing CCTV → floor measurements → evidence-led review
sections.narration: Meet Floorsight, our entry for the OpenCV AI Competition. We help safety teams measure forklift risk from existing cameras, check the evidence, and review a warning before alerting a supervisor.

sections.title: A camera can make a safe gap look dangerous
sections.note: Recorded factory footage · floor estimates depend on calibration
sections.narration: A worker can look almost touching a forklift in a camera image, while being metres away on the floor. Pixel distance can create misleading alarms. Floorsight maps the scene onto the floor, so a reviewer gets an estimated distance and its uncertainty.

sections.title: OpenCV 5 turns images into useful measurements
sections.note: Offline perception · published, privacy-filtered development clip
sections.narration: OpenCV five handles camera geometry, motion, tracking, risk zones, privacy filtering and video. Separate PyTorch models detect people, forklifts and loads. We estimate a close pass, including stopping distance, turning space and hidden areas. Real footage is processed offline; this is not live braking.

sections.title: One warning. Evidence a reviewer can inspect.
sections.note: Historical app recording · local policy · scripted recorded approvals
sections.narration: Here is the working dashboard replaying recorded factory footage. A warning links the camera view, floor map, measurements and review history. The agent requests a short replay, a close-up and a second measurement. A reviewer can inspect the evidence, then approve or reject the warning.

sections.title: The evidence changes the next action
lines: Check recent motion → request a closer look
Conflict or missing evidence → human review
sections.note: Current code · guarded local policy · every tool decision is traced
sections.narration: The agent does more than describe a picture. Visual evidence changes what it asks for and recommends next. A tracking jump alone cannot dismiss a hazard. Conflicting or missing measurements stay uncertain. Floor-warning alerts require human approval. The demonstrated planner is local; live Bedrock access remains blocked by account settings.

sections.title: Fewer false alerts in controlled tests
sections.note: Synthetic two-camera scenes · actual in-memory agent alert records
sections.narration: In controlled two-camera scenes, false exit alerts fell from eight to zero, while all eight visible hazards still produced alerts. All sixteen cases without a second camera went to human review. These are executable synthetic tests with saved evidence and traces, not a field accuracy claim.

sections.title: Uncertainty must not become a false dismissal
sections.note: 80 synthetic cases · all still require human review · no workload claim
sections.narration: On eighty synthetic floor warnings, hazardous rejection recommendations fell from sixteen to zero. False candidates recommended for action fell by forty percent. All cases still require review. We count uncertainty as actionable, so the score cannot improve just by hiding difficult cases.

sections.title: Can control change the outcome?
sections.note: Saved 24 October simulation · a simulated truck, not a real vehicle
sections.narration: To test intervention, we built a simulated warehouse. Without control, the forklift contacts two people who enter its path. This lets us test feedback from vision to movement without claiming that software can stop a truck in recorded video.

sections.title: Two in-path contacts became zero
sections.note: Saved run: 27 m travelled instead of 80 m in 40 s · throughput tradeoff
sections.narration: With control on, both in-path contacts were avoided in that saved scenario. The cost was slower work: twenty-seven metres travelled instead of eighty in forty seconds. The system cannot prevent every contact, or react to a person no camera sees. Real forklift integration has not been performed.

sections.title: A complete vision-to-review system on AWS
sections.note: COOL OpenCV on four Graviton4 cores · private access through SSM
sections.narration: The architecture connects cameras, OpenCV perception, floor-risk estimates and the review agent on an AWS Graviton instance using COOL. S3 stores evidence, DynamoDB keeps track history, CloudWatch records activity, and SNS delivers approved alerts. The recorded AWS run exercised all four adapters.

sections.title: COOL: measured value, with the limits visible
sections.note: Same Graviton host · build/path receipts · no overall speedup claim
sections.narration: For the COOL track, we publish the imported build, Graviton configuration and baseline comparisons. The historical OpenCV chain improved by one point one times, but full perception did not improve. New quality-checked experiments also found no meaningful pipeline speedup. Detector inference remains the main bottleneck.

sections.title: Inspect it. Run it. Deploy it.
lines: 306 passing tests on Linux and Windows
Public simulator + evaluation scripts + raw receipts
sections.note: 2 existing test skips · private footage requires separate access
sections.narration: The public repository includes a self-contained simulator, three hundred and six passing tests on both Linux and Windows, evaluation scripts, model revisions and raw receipts. Terraform, bootstrap code and a deployment guide are included for AWS. No private footage or credentials are needed to run the simulator.

sections.title: Useful measurements. Reviewable decisions.
lines: Agentic Vision + Best Use of COOL
sections.note: Footage: Önal & Dandıl (2024) · CC BY 4.0 · trimmed/pixelated · no endorsement
sections.narration: Floorsight turns existing cameras into measured, reviewable safety evidence. Our contribution is the combination of floor geometry, an evidence-driven agent and human control. The code, deployment instructions, demo and limitations are public. The next step is independent labelled footage and testing with real safety teams.
